original_question: Find a proof that the irrationality measure of zeta(2) is finite without using the prime number theorem. Such a proof would give a route to deriving infinitude-of-primes information from the Euler product for zeta(2) without appealing to the prime number theorem inside the irrationality argument itself.
target_in_paper: The draft targets Section 2009.2.4, "Infinitude of Primes," whose exact problem statement is: "I’m looking for a proof of the finiteness of the irrationality measure of ζ(2) that doesn’t assume the prime number theorem." ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper very closely: it is specifically about ζ(2), it asks for a proof that its irrationality measure is finite, and it explicitly requires avoiding the prime number theorem. It also preserves the surrounding motivation in the paper, namely that ζ(2)=π^2/6 and its Euler product connect irrationality information to information about primes. ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
missing_details: The paper is narrowly about the single value ζ(2)=π^2/6, not about ζ(s) in general or irrationality measures of other constants. ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

To make the question stand-alone, "finite irrationality measure" should be spelled out in Diophantine-approximation terms: one seeks a finite real number μ such that |ζ(2)-p/q|<q^{-μ} has only finitely many solutions in reduced rationals p/q, i.e. coprime integers p and q>=1. The paper alludes to this only informally by saying "if we knew how well π^2 can be approximated by rationals." ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

If one uses the equivalent eventual-lower-bound phrasing, the quantifiers should be explicit: there should exist μ<∞ and q0 such that for all coprime integers p and q with q>=q0, one has |ζ(2)-p/q|>=q^{-μ}. The paper leaves these quantifiers implicit. ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

The restriction "without using the prime number theorem" should be understood globally: the desired proof should avoid any PNT input inside the irrationality-measure argument. The nearby context specifically notes that the existing bound quoted in the paper uses PNT to estimate lcm(1,...,n). ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))

The remarks about deriving information on prime spacings or on π(x) from the Euler product are motivation in the paper, not part of the formal problem statement, so they should not be built into the core research question itself. ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
refined_question: Can one prove, without any use of the prime number theorem, that ζ(2)=π^2/6 has finite irrationality measure; that is, can one show that there exists a finite real number μ such that the inequality |ζ(2)-p/q|<q^{-μ} has only finitely many solutions in coprime integers p and q with q>=1? ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
justification: The relevant target is not a broader neighboring problem but the specific problem-session entry 2009.2.4 on p. 5. The surrounding context there says that the Euler product for ζ(2) links irrationality to infinitude-of-primes information, notes the quoted upper bound 5.441243 for the irrationality exponent of π^2, and explains that the known proof uses the prime number theorem through estimates for lcm(1,...,n). That makes your draft essentially correct already; the main improvements needed are only to formalize what "finite irrationality measure" means, to restrict to reduced rationals, and to keep the prime-counting discussion as motivation rather than as part of the mathematical statement. ([web.williams.edu](https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/math/papers/CANTProblemSessions.pdf))
